title.en: Egill's Nithing-Pole: The Horse-Head Curse Against King and Queen
title.zh: 埃吉爾的誹謗木樁：對國王與王后的馬頭詛咒

region.en: Bergthorsknoll? - the shore by Borg, Iceland

texts.period: Egils saga Skallagrimssonar 13th century (events set c. 900-960); principal MSS 14th c.; English: W. C. Green, The Life and Death of Cormac? - of Egil Skallagrimsson, 1893

source.work: Egils saga ch. 57 (the nithing-pole at Bergthorsknoll? - the shore); ed. Islenzk Fornrit II (1933); English: Green 1893

texts.license: Public domain (Green 1893); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Egill Skallagrimsson, robbed of theinheritance-wergild? - of the inheritance by the king Erik Bloodaxe's law, lands near the king's? - near Borg, cuts a hazel-pole, sets a horse's head on it, and speaks the curse - the formula the saga preserves: 'I set up this nithing-pole and turn this nithing against King Erik and Queen Gunnhildr' - and he turns the horse-head landward and says: 'drive the land-spirits? - 'the? - landwights? - 'wandering? - 'so? - 'that? - 'none? - 'shall? - rest? - 'till? - they? - 'have? - 'driven? - 'Erik? - 'and? - 'Gunnhildr? - 'from? - 'the? - land - the record is the corpus's most famous curse-instrument: the horse-head pole as legal-ritual technology, and the doctrine of the land-spirits as enforceable by any poet with a pole.
summary.zh: 埃吉爾·斯卡拉格里姆森的遺產被國王埃里克·血斧以法令奪走。他在博格附近登岸，砍下榛木杆，頂上馬頭，念出薩迦所載的詛咒套語：「我立起這根誹謗木樁，將它對準埃里克國王與岡希爾德王后」——又把馬頭轉向內陸說道：「驅使大地精靈浪遊四散，直到他們把埃里克和岡希爾德趕出這片土地為止。」此記錄是語料中最著名的詛咒器具：馬頭木樁作為法律—儀式技術，並闡明土地精靈可由任何手持木樁的詩人加以調遣。

texts.canonical_translation: W. C. Green, The Life and Death of Egil Skallagrimsson? - The Saga of Egil Skallagrimsson, London 1893 (public domain); Islenzk Fornrit II

narrative.en:
The nithing-pole episode is the saga's most-cited legal-magic scene, and its full procedure is documented. The grievance: Egill's father? - Skallagrim's inheritance is claimed by the king's law (the Berg-onth? - the judgment at Gula-thing? - Erik's confiscation), and Egill, en route to Iceland, is storm-driven to the shore near Borg. The procedure: 'he? - took? - a? - hazel? - pole? - 'and? - 'went? - on? - a? - rock? - 'crag? - 'so? - 'that? - he? - 'looked? - inland? - 'and? - seaward? - 'and? - 'took? - a? - horse's? - head? - 'and? - 'set? - on? - the? - pole? - 'then? - he? - 'made? - the? - formula? - 'and? - 'spoke: 'here? - I? - set? - up? - a? - nithing-pole? - (nidstong)? - 'and? - 'turn? - 'this? - nithing? - against? - King? - Erik? - 'and? - Queen? - Gunnhildr? - 'then? - he? - 'turned? - the? - horse's? - head? - landward? - 'and? - 'spoke: 'and? - I? - turn? - this? - nithing? - against? - the? - land-spirits? - (landvættir)? - 'that? - dwell? - in? - this? - land? - 'that? - they? - may? - all? - go? - astray? - 'neither? - to? - find? - nor? - rest? - 'their? - resting? - places? - 'till? - they? - 'drive? - Erik? - and? - Gunnhildr? - from? - this? - land - the curse's two addresses: the royals named, and the land-spirits as the enforcing agents.

The law-theory: the saga's pole-curse is the formalized nith - the defamation-ritual: the pole is the legal document of a curse, and its grammar is juridical (naming, address, agent, condition). The saga's context: Egill was a landowner-poet whose law-fare with the king ran through a lifetime; the pole is his extraterritorial remedy - the curse as lawsuit filed with the land itself. And the land-spirits doctrine: the landvættir are the country's resident guardians (the same beings that, in other records, guard Iceland's coasts - the saga elsewhere documents their power: the dragon, the bird, the bull, the giant at the? - the four quarters) - and the poet's claim is that they are enforceable: a wronged man with a pole may displace them and drive the regime out.

The record's cultural functions are the pole-curse technology and the land-spirit enforceability doctrine. The nidstong is the corpus's signature curse-instrument (documented also in the runic curse-stones and in the sagas' other pole-scenes), and its procedure - hazel, horse-head, formula, landward turn - is the most complete in the record. And the doctrine: the land's spirits are legal agents - the landscape itself is a court of enforcement. In the atlas, the record anchors the curse-pole family (the Roman? - the frame is defamatory ritual: each a formalized curse; the Norse one is distinctive in the horse-head and the land-spirit agency.

functions: Pole-curse technology: hazel-pole, horse-head, juridical formula, landward turn
Nith as legal document: the curse filed as a lawsuit with the land itself
Land-spirit enforceability: the landvættir as the curse's agents
Extraterritorial remedy: the wronged poet's pole against royal law

title.en: Andvari's Ring: The Curse of the Dwarf's Gold
title.zh: 安德瓦利的指環：矮人黃金的詛咒

region.en: The falls of Andvari and the Rhine-road (symbolic pin at Rhine valley)
region.zh: 安德瓦利瀑布與萊茵之路（象徵性定位於萊茵河谷）

texts.period: Reginsmal c. 1000-1200; Volsunga saga chs. 1-14 (13th c.); principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to, NKS 1824 b 4to

source.work: Reginsmal; Volsunga saga chs. 1-14; English: Bellows 1923; Morris & Magnusson 1870

texts.license: Public domain (Bellows 1923; Morris & Magnusson 1870); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Loki, hunting with Odin and Hoenir, kills the otter - who is the dwarf Andvari's son Otr in otter-shape; the weregild demanded by Hreidmar is the otter-skin filled and covered with gold. Loki takes the dwarf Andvari (fishing in the falls as a pike), seizes his whole hoard, and Andvari - robbed - lays the curse on the ring Andvaranaut: 'the ring? - 'shall? - 'be? - 'the? - 'death? - 'of? - 'all? - 'who? - 'own? - 'it? - and the gold's curse works through the cycle: Hreidmar killed by Fafnir and Regin; Fafnir becomes a dragon on the hoard; Sigurd wins and dies of it; the Rhine sinks the gold. The record is the corpus's central curse-charter: gold as a circulating death-sentence, and the weregild's irony - the compensation-payment becomes the family's destroyer.
summary.zh: 洛基與奧丁、海尼爾同行狩獵時，殺死了一頭水獺——那正是矮人安德瓦利之子奧特所化。赫萊德瑪索要的贖罪金，須將水獺皮裝滿、覆滿黃金。洛基捉住在瀑布中化為梭子魚垂釣的矮人安德瓦利，奪其全部藏金；安德瓦利被奪後，對指環安德瓦利奧特施下詛咒：「凡持有此環者，皆將因它而死。」詛咒循傳說週期運轉：赫萊德瑪死於法夫納與雷金之手；法夫納化為巨龍盤踞藏金；西格魯德得金而亡；黃金終沉萊茵河底。此記錄是語料的核心詛咒憲章：黃金即流轉的死刑判決，而贖罪金的反諷在於——賠償之物反而滅絕了整個家族。

texts.canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Volsunga saga via Morris & Magnusson 1870

narrative.en:
The Andvari-curse is the Sigurd-cycle's economic engine, and its charter is laid in the cycle's first generation. The kill: the three gods walking see an otter with a salmon? - Otr, Hreidmar's son, in otter-shape; Loki kills it with a stone - and Hreidmar's weregild: the otter-skin filled with gold and covered over 'nose? - 'and? - 'every? - hair? - the payment's impossible precision. The extraction: Loki takes Andvari (the dwarf fishing as a pike? - in the falls, the dwarf who 'lived? - 'in? - 'a? - stone? - 'and? - 'was? - 'rich? - 'as? - 'a? - 'pike? - 'in? - the? - falls), seizes his hoard, and leaves him the ring Andvaranaut - and the dwarf's curse is the record's charter: 'the? - ring? - 'shall? - 'be? - 'the? - 'death? - 'of? - 'every? - one? - 'that? - owns? - it? - 'and? - 'the? - gold? - 'likewise? - the weregild is paid - and the curse enters circulation.

The curse's working is the cycle's plot: Hreidmar, paid, is killed by Fafnir and Regin ('a? - 'father's? - death? - 'for? - the? - hoard); Fafnir takes the hoard to Gnita-heath and becomes a dragon - the gold's holder literally shape-shifts into its keeper-beast; Sigurd slays him and takes the ring; and the cycle's deaths run (Sigurd, Gunnar, Hogni, Atli, the sons); the gold ends in the Rhine - 'and? - 'the? - Rhine? - 'shall? - 'rule? - 'the? - rings - Gunnar's line - and the curse's circuit closes where the gold sank. The record's cultural functions are the gold-as-death-sentence doctrine and the weregild-irony doctrine. The curse-charter makes gold a circulating sentence: each holder's death is the ring's clause executed, and the economy of the whole heroic corpus (the Niflung-cycle) is legal-economically structured by it - the weregild, the north's legal payment, becomes the family's destroyer: compensation transmuted into contagion. And the otter-weregild's symbolism: the payment is demanded in the shape of the victim - the legal debt measured in the victim's own skin.

In the atlas, the record anchors the cursed-treasure family (the Greek Polydoros-gold, the Mesopotamian? - each a hoard with a death-clause; the Norse one is distinctive in the weregild-frame and the dragon-transformation.

The curse's mechanics run through the whole cycle as a legal ledger: each holder's death is the ring's clause executed (Hreidmar killed for the hoard, Fafnir transformed by it, Sigurd murdered for it, the Gjukungs destroyed with it, Atli killed by it), and the saga's arithmetic - 'the ring shall be the death of everyone that owns it' - is the Niflung-cycle's plot-generator: the treasure's biography is a death-register. And the weregild-frame is the doctrine's legal genius: the curse is installed at the moment of legal payment, so the north's own compensation-institution (the weregild that settles feuds) becomes the mechanism of its greatest feud - the myth's critique of the gold-economy stated in law's own terms. The record thus anchors the cursed-treasure family: gold as circulating sentence, installed by the robbed and executed by the paid.

functions: Gold-as-death-sentence: the curse as a circulating clause executed in each holder
Weregild-irony: the legal payment becomes the family's destroyer
Dragon-transformation: the hoard's keeper shape-shifts into its beast
Rhine-deposit closure: the curse's circuit ends where the gold sank

title.en: Tyrfing's Curse: The Sword That Must Kill Each Time It Is Drawn
title.zh: 提爾芬之詛咒：出鞘必須見血的寶劍

region.en: The forge of Dvalin and Durin (symbolic pin at Samsø, Denmark)
region.zh: 德瓦林與都林的鍛爐（象徵性定位於丹麥薩姆索島）

texts.period: Hervarar saga ok Heidreks 13th century (verse of older heroic date); English: Kershaw 1921; Tolkien 1960

source.work: Hervarar saga ok Heidreks (the forging of Tyrfing); ed. Rafn; English trans. Kershaw 1921; Tolkien 1960

texts.license: Public domain (Kershaw 1921); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: King Svafrlami forces the dwarfs Dvalin and Durin to forge him a sword with a gold hilt, never failing, never rusting, cutting stone and iron as cloth - and they forge it under duress. At the gate the king says 'the sword? - 'the? - work? - shall? - 'be? - 'as? - 'I? - 'bade? - the dwarfs answer: the blade shall be the death of a man each time it is drawn, three shameful deeds each time? - and it shall be Svafrlami's own bane - and they vanish. The curse works exactly: Svafrlami dies by it (Angantyr's hand); it kills whenever drawn through three generations (Arngrim's sons' berserk-duel, Heidrek's crimes, the final battle); and Hervor's mound-claim gives it its last biography. The record is the corpus's weapon-curse charter: a forged object with a contractual kill-clause, and the doctrine that a weapon taken by force pays in its owners' blood.
summary.zh: 斯瓦弗爾拉米王強令矮人德瓦林與都林為他鍛造一柄寶劍：金柄、永不失手、永不生鏽、斬石鐵如斬布——矮人被迫在脅迫下鍛成。城門前，國王稱讚寶劍「正如我所命」，矮人答道：此劍每出鞘一次必奪一命，每次還要犯下三件可恥之事，而且它終將成為斯瓦弗爾拉米自己的死劫——言畢消失。詛咒分毫不差地應驗：斯瓦弗爾拉米死於此劍；三代之間，出鞘必見血（阿恩格里姆諸子的狂戰士決鬥、海德里克的罪行、最後的決戰）；赫爾沃的探墓之舉更為其添上最後的傳記。此記錄是語料的兵器詛咒憲章：一把帶有契約殺戮條款的鍛造之物——以強力奪得的兵器，必以持有者的血償還。

texts.canonical_translation: Nora Kershaw Chadwick, Stories and Ballads of the Far Past, Cambridge 1921 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The Tyrfing-charter is the fornaldarsaga's weapon-curse doctrine in its purest form. The forging: Svafrlami 'caught? - the dwarfs 'as? - 'they? - 'came? - 'out? - of? - the? - stone? - 'at? - dusk? - 'and? - 'forced? - them? - 'to? - forge? - 'a? - sword: 'a? - hilt? - of? - gold, 'never? - failing? - 'of? - blow? - 'nor? - rusting, 'that? - would? - 'cut? - stone? - and? - iron? - 'as? - 'though? - 'it? - were? - cloth? - the specification's perfection is the curse's mechanism: a perfect sword can only be a death-instrument. The curse's terms are contractual: 'when? - 'the? - king? - 'said? - 'the? - work? - 'was? - 'as? - 'he? - bade? - 'the? - dwarfs? - said: 'the? - sword? - 'shall? - 'be? - 'the? - 'death? - 'of? - 'a? - man? - 'each? - 'time? - 'it? - 'is? - drawn? - 'and? - 'three? - 'shameful? - 'deeds? - 'with? - 'it? - each? - time? - 'and? - 'it? - shall? - 'be? - 'thy? - 'own? - 'bane? - 'and? - they? - 'went? - 'into? - the? - rock? - the kill-clause, the shame-clause, and the suicide-clause, addressed to the forced buyer.

The curse's working through three generations is the saga's plot-architecture: Svafrlami dies by it (Angantyr's? - Arngrim's? - the first killing); the sword passes to Arngrim and his berserk-sons (the Samsø-duel, the mound-burial); Hervor's claim wakes it; Heidrek's crimes (the shame-clause in each drawing) and the riddle-contest's collapse (Odin's death-sentence); and the end: Angantyr kills Hlod - the brothers' war as the sword's last accounting. The record's cultural functions are the forced-purchase doctrine and the perfect-weapon paradox. The curse's terms are addressed to the buyer who forced the sale: the weapon taken by duress carries its seller's revenge as a contract - the myth-world's theory of duress in exchange. And the perfect-weapon paradox: the sword's specifications (never failing, cutting as cloth) are the very terms of the curse - perfection in a weapon is its kill-clause: the better the sword, the more deaths it must deliver.

In the atlas, the record anchors the weapon-curse family (the Chinese? - the frame is cursed blades: the Japanese Muramasa's blood-hunger, the Greek? - each a weapon with a kill-clause; the Norse one is distinctive in its contractual terms and the shame-counter.

functions: Contractual kill-clause: the curse as terms addressed to the forced buyer
Perfect-weapon paradox: the sword's specifications are the curse's mechanism
Shame-counter: three shameful deeds with each drawing
Three-generation accounting: the curse's biography runs through the whole saga

title.en: Hrafnkel's Freyfaxi: The God's Horse and the Broken Taboo
title.zh: 赫拉芬克爾的弗雷髮鬃：神之馬與被破除的禁忌

region.zh: 冰島東部赫拉芬克爾谷阿達爾博爾

texts.period: Hrafnkels saga Freysgoda 14th century (older material); ed. Islenzk Fornrit XI (1950)

source.work: Hrafnkels saga Freysgoda; ed. Islenzk Fornrit XI (1950); English in various saga-collections

texts.license: Public domain (older editions); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Hrafnkel, a chieftain dedicated to Freyr, builds a great temple and dedicates to the god half his best livestock - including the stallion Freyfaxi - and binds himself with an oath: he will kill any man who rides Freyfaxi or uses the dedicated animals. The oath is enforced: he kills the shepherd who rides the horse. The farmer Samr hires men, captures Hrafnkel, and hangs him over the? - in the? - on the rope? - but lets him live on the condition of giving up the dale - and they ride Freyfaxi and slaughter the dedicated animals; and the saga's quiet doctrine: Freyr does nothing - the god's power, so terrorizing in the oath, is absent at the taboo's breaking. The record is the corpus's best taboo-case-study: a cult-taboo sworn, enforced by murder, and broken - and the god's silence as the saga's own thesis.
summary.zh: 獻身於弗雷的酋長赫拉芬克爾建起大神廟，將最好的牲畜一半獻給神明——包括種馬弗雷髮鬃——並立下誓言：凡騎弗雷髮鬃或使用獻祭牲畜者，一律格殺。誓言嚴厲執行：騎馬的牧羊人被處死。農夫薩姆爾僱人擒獲赫拉芬克爾，本要吊死他，後改為饒其性命，條件是放棄整個山谷——隨後眾人騎上弗雷髮鬃，宰殺獻祭牲畜。而薩迦平靜地寫下了它的論點：弗雷毫無作為——誓言中那令人生畏的神力，在禁忌被破之際竟消失無蹤。此記錄是語料中最佳的禁忌案例研究：一個立誓、殺人執行、又被打破的崇拜禁忌——而神的沉默正是薩迦自己的論點。

texts.canonical_translation: Hrafnkels saga Freysgoda, Islenzk Fornrit XI, Reykjavik 1950; paraphrase

narrative.en:
The Hrafnkel-saga is the saga corpus's tightest novella, and its taboo-plot is the corpus's best case-study of a cult's power-claims. The dedication: Hrafnkel 'loved? - no? - 'he? - 'worshipped? - Freyr? - 'above? - all? - other? - gods? - 'and? - 'gave? - him? - 'a? - half? - of? - his? - best? - livestock? - 'the? - temple? - at? - A-dale? - 'and? - 'the? - stallion? - Freyfaxi? - 'with? - 'the? - mane? - 'of? - 'the? - god's? - name? - the horse dedicated by name? - 'and? - the oath: 'he? - vowed? - 'that? - 'he? - 'would? - 'be? - 'the? - slayer? - of? - 'any? - man? - who? - 'rode? - Freyfaxi? - 'or? - used? - 'the? - dedicated? - animals? - without? - his? - leave? - the taboo's kill-clause sworn.

The enforcement: the shepherd Porbjorn rides Freyfaxi; the stallion 'runs? - 'to? - the? - temple? - 'and? - 'neighs? - the horse's complaint to its god - and Hrafnkel kills the shepherd 'at? - the? - door? - of? - 'his? - tent? - the taboo enforced by murder, and the god's stallion testifying. The broken taboo: Samr, the poor farmer whose brother was the shepherd, hires men, takes Hrafnkel in his sleep, hangs him over the? - from the? - rope? - and spares him only on terms: the dale given up, the animals? - 'and? - they? - 'rode? - Freyfaxi? - 'and? - 'slaughtered? - 'the? - dedicated? - beasts? - 'and? - 'took? - the? - temple's? - goods? - 'and? - 'Freyr? - 'did? - nothing? - the saga's pointed clause: 'and? - no? - one? - was? - 'the? - worse? - 'for? - it? - the god's silence at the taboo's breaking is the saga's thesis: the cult's power-claims are the chieftain's politics, and the taboo's enforcement is lawless killing - the saga's genre is the legal unmasking of a cult.

The record's cultural functions are the taboo-case-study doctrine and the god's-silence thesis. passages.text: Hrafnkel worshipped Freyr above all gods and dedicated to him half his best livestock, including the stallion Freyfaxi; and he vowed to slay any man who rode Freyfaxi or used the dedicated animals without leave. When the shepherd rode the horse, Hrafnkel killed him; but later Samr took Hrafnkel, spared his life on terms, rode Freyfaxi and slaughtered the dedicated beasts - and Freyr did nothing, and no one was the worse for it.

summary.en: Among the Blekinge stones - Stentoften and Björketorp - stand carved curse-formulas of the 7th century, the north's earliest datable curse-instruments. The Björketorp text (per the standard readings): 'the? - prophecy? - 'of? - 'destruction? - 'I? - 'foresee? - 'the? - 'mighty? - 'destruction? - 'of? - 'the? - 'man? - 'who? - 'breaks? - 'this? - 'monument? - 'in? - 'memory? - 'of? - 'the? - dead? - 'the? - row? - of? - runes? - 'is? - 'the? - 'guard? - 'and? - 'the? - 'stone? - 'the? - 'grave? - the record is the runic curse-doctrine: the stones as a liturgy of protection, and the mover of the monument as its target - the earliest Swedish curse-law in stone.

narrative.en:
The Blekinge stones are Scandinavia's oldest curse-instruments, and their doctrine is protection-by-writing. The stones: Stentoften (DR 357) and Björketorp (DR 360), standing in pairs? - in line across the landscape, carved in the 7th century with memorial-formulas and curse-formulas; the Björketorp text (standard readings): 'uþarba? - spia? - 'the? - prophecy? - of? - destruction? - 'gud? - 'runar? - 'the? - row? - of? - runes? - 'the? - readings: 'I? - foresee? - destruction? - 'for? - 'the? - one? - 'who? - 'breaks? - 'the? - 'stone? - 'in? - 'memory? - 'of? - 'the? - dead? - 'the? - curse's target is the mover - 'the? - monument's? - protection is its law, and the rune-row is named as the guard: 'the? - row? - of? - runes? - 'is? - 'the? - 'ward? - 'and? - 'the? - stone? - 'is? - 'the? - grave? - the doctrine: writing is protection, and the monument is its own body.

The record's cultural functions are the runic-curse doctrine and the monument-law doctrine. The Blekinge formulae are the earliest Swedish curse-law in stone - a society protecting its graves (and its land-claims) by written threat, two centuries before the Viking-age runestones' curses ('the? - 'vargr? - 'i? - ve? - 'the? - outlaw-clauses of Glavendrup and Tryggevælde - the later descendants of this doctrine). And the monument-law: the stone is both grave-marker and legal instrument - the dead's claim on the land written as a threat, the ancestor's property-right in curse-form.

In the atlas, the record anchors the grave-curse family (the Greek? - the frame is tomb-curses: each a monument protecting its own dead; the Blekinge one is distinctive in runic form and the mover-target.

The Blekinge monument-line's full apparatus (Stentofor's memorial-clauses and initiation-formulae beside Bjorketorp's threat) documents the stones' double office: they mark a ritual site (the bracteate-hoard's context suggests a cult-place) and protect it by written law - the 7th-century society's legal theology in stone. And the curse's addressee is precise: not the general thief but the mover of the monument - the one act that would erase the claim - so the curse is property-law in threat-form: the ancestor's title defended against relocation. The record thus anchors the early runic corpus's legal range: the futhark's dedications, the Rok stone's mythic archive, and the Blekinge stones' curse-law - one alphabet's three registers.

The stones' monument-group completes the doctrine: the Blekinge pair stands in a designed line across the landscape (the sight-line documented by the surveys), and the rune-rows' placement - face, side, top of the stones - documents the carving's ceremonial care: the curse is not graffiti but architecture. And the doctrine's descendants complete the record: the Viking-age curse-clauses (the outlaw-formulas of Glavendrup and Tryggevalde, the Thor-hallowing of Velanda) descend from this 7th-century law - the runic alphabet's legal register continuous from the pre-Viking monuments to the Christian-era stones. The record thus anchors the grave-curse family: writing as protection, the monument as its own body, and the mover of stones as the law's target.
